title: Cells architecture
caveat: Capabilities vary by model, and whole-cell integration is ongoing. No single run uses every part drawn here.

statuses.label: Qualified or judged
statuses.description: Numerically qualified (a registered protocol passed) or judged (used in a registered experiment), in its declared scope.

statuses.label: Implemented and guarded
statuses.description: On main with its tests and guards: the plan's 'implemented' and 'guarded' levels. Not yet qualified by a registered protocol.

statuses.label: Established
statuses.description: Built earlier and in routine use: older model families and shared infrastructure. Scope and evidence are in each guide.

statuses.label: Designed
statuses.description: A design or protocol is written or accepted; the code is not on main.

statuses.label: Planned
statuses.description: Named in the plan or roadmap, or decided by the user; not started.

statuses.label: Failed qualification
statuses.description: Built, then failed its registered qualification. Kept as evidence and not relied on.

statuses.label: External reference
statuses.description: Outside the engine: a reference simulator or data set, run out of process and compared through saved outputs.

representations.label: Simulated
representations.description: The engine evolves this state step by step, with material, charge and energy accounted for.

representations.label: Modelled in aggregate
representations.description: Represented as a population, count or rate law, not as individual molecules. Shapes drawn for it are illustrations.

representations.label: Prescribed
representations.description: Happens on a schedule the experiment sets; the cell does not decide it.

representations.label: Illustration only
representations.description: Drawn for orientation. Nothing in the engine stands behind it yet.

model_groups.label: Composite tissue model
model_groups.description: resolved_pump_composite@1: the pump tissue model's own step plus declared operators. These parts run together in one model today. Its inner tissue model was rebuilt in place as one modular model, which landed on main on 16 November 2026.

model_groups.label: Earlier tissue families
model_groups.description: The older resolved-tissue families, one module per feature combination. Calcium, fuel, mitochondria, regulation and repair run together here. Their physics moves into the composite model in stages, as uses need it (D167).

model_groups.label: Separate engines
model_groups.description: Models that run on their own: vertex mechanics and the regulatory circuits.

relation_kinds.label: uses
relation_kinds.description: The first part imports the second in the source code.

relation_kinds.label: is an operator of
relation_kinds.description: Registered as an operator of the composite model.

relation_kinds.label: requires
relation_kinds.description: The operator declares that this law must come before it.

relation_kinds.label: writes
relation_kinds.description: The operator declares that it changes this state and books the change.

relation_kinds.label: provides
relation_kinds.description: The operator provides this state to the rest of the model as its current value.

relation_kinds.label: reads
relation_kinds.description: The operator reads a value another operator provides.

relation_kinds.label: cannot combine with
relation_kinds.description: The composite refuses this pair: one operator reads a value as declared while the other changes it, or both provide the same value.

relation_kinds.label: wraps
relation_kinds.description: The composite runs this model's own step.

relation_kinds.label: runs
relation_kinds.description: The experiment runs this engine model or operator.

relation_kinds.label: would extend
relation_kinds.description: A planned or designed part, and what it builds on.

relation_kinds.label: delivers
relation_kinds.description: A plan gate, or a round of work, and a part it is meant to deliver.

relation_kinds.label: is implemented by
relation_kinds.description: A capability and the engine parts behind it.

relation_kinds.label: has its law in
relation_kinds.description: The engine law that acts on this unit is in this part of the engine (from the law inventory, checked against the code).

relation_kinds.label: is drawn in the cell view as
relation_kinds.description: The part of the cell view that stands for this unit.

groups.label: Execution
groups.description: How a definition becomes a checked, restartable run.

groups.label: Numerics
groups.description: Time stepping, field solves and long-time methods.

groups.label: Shared state
groups.description: The entities that own physical state. Mechanisms that affect the same thing change the same state.

groups.label: Physical laws
groups.description: Transport, kinetics, chemistry, geometry and mechanics, one law per module.

groups.label: Models
groups.description: Versioned model families built from the laws.

groups.label: Operators
groups.description: Laws declared as operators of the composite tissue model.

groups.label: Experiments
groups.description: Clients of the engine: parity checks, morphogenesis, division and heredity.

groups.label: References and validation
groups.description: Outside the engine: reference simulators run out of process, independent reference solutions and the test gate.

groups.label: Plan gates
groups.description: The current plan's gates, in order, from docs/CURRENT_PLAN.md.

proteins.title: Protein atlas
proteins.summary: From Cells' own law inventory, with links out to the public protein atlases. The inventory has 49 units. One of them, an engineered protein cage, is left out of the picture for now: it is a designed protein, not a part of a cell.
proteins.caveat: Shapes are schematic, drawn from subunit counts, and not to scale. A grey form is a generic law: no protein is assigned.

review.text: Reviews on 14 and 15 November 2026 found no channel, pump, transporter or junction law among them. Two cases are the lead's to classify: secretion and uptake across a membrane, and the binding of molecules to sites.

mappings.label: Assigned in source
mappings.description: The law, its documents or the source it cites names the protein. This records a label; the kind of evidence on each law says what stands behind it.

mappings.label: Candidate
mappings.description: The law models a named native current or channel class. Which gene products carry it is the inventory's inference.

mappings.label: Generic
mappings.description: The law is deliberately generic, phenomenological or manufactured. Products are listed as candidates only.

evidence.label: Expressed isoform
evidence.description: The cited data come from the named isoform, expressed on its own.

evidence.label: Isoform named in the title
evidence.description: The cited source names the isoform in its title; the inventory read no further detail.

evidence.label: Native current
evidence.description: The cited data are a current recorded from native cells, not from an isolated isoform.

evidence.label: Neuron model
evidence.description: The cited source is a model of a neuron.

evidence.label: Derived reduction
evidence.description: A reduced (Morris-Lecar) form of the named channel.

evidence.label: No detail in the source
evidence.description: The source gives no detail on what the coefficients were measured from.

atlases.label: E. coli
atlases.plain: A rod-shaped bacterium of the animal gut with 4,403 proteins in UniProt's reference proteome of strain K-12. The units of the law inventory are channels, pumps and junctions of animal cells; this is what the same families' signatures find in it.
method: The organism's proteins are the 4,403 reviewed entries of UniProt's reference proteome UP000000625 (release 2026_04), one protein each.
Licences were read before anything was copied; each is stated in sources.

A unit counts as found only where a protein carries the signature of a family that makes the machine itself (the subunit that forms the channel, or the pump's own chain). A protein that carries only the signature of a family that goes with the machine (a regulator, an accessory subunit) is no candidate: the unit's note names it, and it is listed under extra. This reading is the file's own.
Each unit's family was taken from its own human candidates, by the same InterPro signatures that the planarian, Syn3A and M. pneumoniae atlases ask. The build checks that the candidates carry them.
Each signature was looked for among the InterPro entries UniProt gives each of the 4,403 proteins. No unit's own family was found; 1 protein carries the signature of an accessory family alone.
A control for every signature: how many reviewed UniProtKB entries of all bacteria carry it; each unit's note gives what came back.

8 further signatures, of the channels a bacterium could have (potassium, chloride, magnesium, water and membrane-stretch channels), were looked for as well; the 15 proteins that carry them are listed under extra (the potassium channel domain (kch); the large-conductance mechanosensitive channel (MscL) (mscL); the mechanosensitive channel MscS (mscK, mscM, mscS, ybdG, ybiO and ynaI); chloride channels of the ClC family (clcA, clcB and yfeO); aquaporins and their relatives (major intrinsic proteins) (aqpZ and glpF); CorA-type magnesium channels (corA and zntB)), with the cell's P-type ATPases and the catalytic head of its ATP synthase.
No similarity search was run, and nothing is called an ortholog.
The inventory has 49 units. One of them, an engineered protein cage, is left out of the picture for now: it is a designed protein, not a part of a cell. The 48 others are shown and counted here.

atlases.label: Fruit fly
atlases.plain: The fruit fly of the laboratory, with 13,814 genes in UniProt's reference proteome. This is what the family signatures of Cells' units find among the one protein shown for each gene.
method: The fly's proteins are the 13,814 of UniProt's gene-by-gene set of the reference proteome UP000000803 (release 2026_04): one for each gene, 3,850 with a reviewed entry and 9,964 with an unreviewed one.
Licences were read before anything was copied; each is stated in sources.
Each unit's family was taken from its own human candidates, by the same InterPro signatures that the other species' atlases ask. The build checks that the candidates carry them.

Each signature was looked for among the InterPro entries UniProt gives each protein. A unit counts as found only where a protein carries the signature of a family that makes the machine itself; an accessory family alone does not make it found.
Where no protein carries the family the engine's law names and proteins carry another family asked for the same machine (innexins, for gap junctions), the finding is 'different family'.

Each product says, apart, how it was found and what its entry is. Found: by the signature of a family that makes the machine itself, which makes it a candidate by family, or only by that of a family that goes with the machine (a regulator, or a subunit that makes no channel or pump by itself), which makes it no candidate for the machine's own work. Its entry: reviewed by a curator, or annotated automatically; that says how the entry was written, not that the protein does the unit's work.
Several units of one family (the Kv1 channels) list the same proteins, and nothing here says which protein does which unit's work.
No similarity search was run, and nothing is called an ortholog.
The inventory has 49 units. One of them, an engineered protein cage, is left out of the picture for now: it is a designed protein, not a part of a cell. The 48 others are shown and counted here.

atlases.label: Planarian
atlases.plain: A freshwater flatworm that regrows its whole body from a fragment; it is the planarian the databases know best, with 1,588 UniProtKB entries, more than all other planarians together, and a chromosome-scale genome with predicted genes.
method: Species: UniProt holds 1,588 entries for Schmidtea mediterranea (4 reviewed), more than half of the 2,784 it holds for all planarians (the order Tricladida; among the others, Dugesia japonica 499, Girardia tigrina 81, Schmidtea polychroa 74, Dugesia ryukyuensis 23), and a proteome for no planarian. WormBase ParaSite holds a chromosome-scale genome assembly of Schmidtea mediterranea with gene models; the assembly is described by Ivanković and others 2024. So the atlas is of Schmidtea mediterranea.
Licences were read before anything was copied; each is stated in sources, and what was read but not copied is in not_copied.

Each unit's family was taken from its own human candidates: the InterPro signatures they carry were read from UniProt, and one or two that mark the family were chosen. The build checks that the candidates carry them.
Curated entries first: UniProt has 4 reviewed entries for the species, and none belongs to a family the atlas draws.
Named in a publication: a planarian protein counts as named only where the saved abstract, or the saved open-access text, of the paper uses the name. 4 products rest on this.

Family signature: unreviewed UniProtKB entries of the species that carry the signature, and gene models that carry it. The gene models are those of one genome annotation (WBPS19 of WormBase ParaSite, assembly schMedS3_haplotype1): 17,294 genes with a predicted protein. The ones the atlas names are listed in data/proteins/planarian/reference_proteins.tsv. A model carries a signature if that annotation's own InterPro matches say so, or if its predicted protein is, letter for letter, a sequence that carries it in UniProt's archive (InterPro 111.0).
A UniProtKB sequence and a gene model are given as one product when at least 80% of the sequence's 8-residue words occur in the model's predicted protein and no other gene reaches half of that share.

Where a signature found nothing, it was also asked of all 98,660 planarian sequences in UniProt's archive, of the UniProtKB entries of all flatworms and of reviewed human entries; the unit's note gives what came back.

Each product says, apart, how it was found (named in a publication, by the signature of a family that makes the machine, or only by that of a family that goes with it, such as a beta subunit or a regulator) and what its record is (a UniProtKB entry, reviewed or not, or a gene model of the genome annotation).

A product found by the signature of a family that makes the machine is a candidate, never an established counterpart; one found only by that of a family that goes with the machine is no candidate for the machine's own work. Counts are gene models in one haplotype of one genome assembly, not genes confirmed in the animal, and short models may be fragments.
No similarity search against other species was run, and no product is called an ortholog.
The inventory has 49 units. One of them, an engineered protein cage, is left out of the picture for now: it is a designed protein, not a part of a cell. The 48 others are shown and counted here.

atlases.label: Thale cress
atlases.plain: A small flowering plant of the laboratory, with 27,368 genes in UniProt's reference proteome. The units of the law inventory are channels, pumps and junctions of animal cells; this is what their family signatures find among the one protein shown for each gene.
method: The plant's proteins are the 27,368 of UniProt's gene-by-gene set of the reference proteome UP000006548 (release 2026_04): one for each gene, 16,212 with a reviewed entry and 11,156 with an unreviewed one.
Licences were read before anything was copied; each is stated in sources.
Each unit's family was taken from its own human candidates, by the same InterPro signatures that the other species' atlases ask. The build checks that the candidates carry them.

Each signature was looked for among the InterPro entries UniProt gives each protein. A unit counts as found only where a protein carries the signature of a family that makes the machine itself; an accessory family alone does not make it found.

A plant has channels and pumps of families of its own, which no unit of the inventory stands for. They are not listed here: the search asks only for the families of Cells' units. 'Different family' is given only where the inventory's table names another family for the same machine, and it names none that a plant has.

Each product says, apart, how it was found and what its entry is. Found: by the signature of a family that makes the machine itself, which makes it a candidate by family, or only by that of a family that goes with the machine (a regulator, or a subunit that makes no channel or pump by itself), which makes it no candidate for the machine's own work. Its entry: reviewed by a curator, or annotated automatically; that says how the entry was written, not that the protein does the unit's work.
Nothing here says which protein does which unit's work.
No similarity search was run, and nothing is called an ortholog.
The inventory has 49 units. One of them, an engineered protein cage, is left out of the picture for now: it is a designed protein, not a part of a cell. The 48 others are shown and counted here.

modelled.text: Cells models a generic cell and a sheet of such cells, with laws whose candidate proteins are named by their human genes; that generic cell is the one drawn. No human cell type, organ or body is modelled yet. The first human cell type is designed, not modelled: a ventricular heart cell, whose laws follow O'Hara and Rudy's model of 2011 (the endocardial cell). Its design note is on main, and its status there reads proposed, with its choices decided by D184 (decisions D183 and D184, 16 November 2026); nothing of it is built yet. The heart and the body are placeholder outlines.

facts.label: Nucleus
facts.value: nuclei isolated from HeLa cells, a human cell line, in the paper's column “HeLa (fresh)”, were 17.18 ± 0.39 µm wide (the mean of their long and short axes, by light microscopy) and 16.20 ± 0.48 µm high (by atomic force microscopy), mean ± s.e.m. of 21 nuclei; the same table's column “HeLa” gives 12.73 ± 0.54 µm wide and 10.91 ± 0.59 µm high (23 nuclei). These are nuclei taken out of the cell, not nuclei measured in an intact cell

facts.label: Mitochondrion
facts.value: the paper's normal mitochondria, beside the giant ones it studies, in the liver of people with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, measured in three dimensions, were 0.55 ± 0.15 µm wide and 1.18 ± 0.59 µm long, total means ± S.D. combining the measurements from each patient (four cells from each patient, 16 cells in all); its giant mitochondria were 0.64 ± 0.24 µm wide and 3.99 ± 1.68 µm long

facts.label: Lysosome
facts.value: single lysosomes of HeLa cells, each measured on its own by electron microscopy guided by fluorescence: one “a spherical shape with an approximate diameter of 560 nm” (0.56 µm), others 0.56 × 0.56 × 0.51 µm, 0.55 × 0.58 × 0.62 µm and 0.66 × 0.69 × 0.50 µm. These are single examples, not a measure of many

facts.label: COPI vesicle
facts.value: dots containing COPI (coatomer) in HeLa cells, seen by STED fluorescence microscopy and sized by fitting each image (a 2D Lorentzian), were 126 ± 15 nm (0.126 µm), n = 181: an apparent size from a light microscope's fit, not an electron microscope's; COPI vesicles made in vitro measured 114 ± 11 nm (n = 64) the same way

facts.label: Peroxisome
facts.value: an encyclopedia's general range, not a measurement in one cell type: “Peroxisomes are small (0.1–1 μm diameter) organelles”

facts.label: Endoplasmic reticulum
facts.value: a review's general figure, not a measurement in one cell type: the reticulum's membrane “is formed into sheets and tubules of roughly 80–100 nm diameter”, and “The sheets are flat, with a bilayer separation of 30–50 nm”, the distance between a sheet's two membranes; the review names no species or cell type there

facts.label: Golgi apparatus
facts.value: a review's general figure for mammalian cells, not a measurement in one cell type: “In mammalian cells, this organelle consists of a pile of flat, disk-like membranes, the cisternae”; “The diameter of the cisternae is also cell type-dependent, and is usually 0.5–1 μm”, and the cisternae of a stack are “usually numbering between 3 and 11”

facts.label: Lipid droplet
facts.value: an encyclopedia's general range, not a measurement in one cell type: “the diameter of lipid droplets ranges from 0.1–5 μm in non-adipocyte cells, but increases to over 100 μm in white adipocytes”

facts.label: Autophagosome
facts.value: an encyclopedia's general range for mammalian cells, not a measurement in one cell type: “An autophagosome is a spherical structure with double layer membranes.” “Yeast autophagosomes are about 500-900 nm, while mammalian autophagosomes are larger (500-1500 nm).” The mammalian range is 0.5–1.5 µm; the sentence carries no reference of its own

modelled.text: The project's record decides that the frog's early cleavage, from one cell to four, is the first subject of its cell-division work (D141, D144, the cell-division plan). That work's design note is on main, and so far the engine has carried an egg-scale cell through prescribed division against independently written references (the Engine view's Cell division S2–S5a). The record's first prediction for the egg itself, J1, its membrane potential at the onset of second cleavage, was made with an independent reference model and misses the measured value (12 November 2026); no engine run of it exists. No model of this egg is registered, so the word here is the lower one the record allows: planned. What is drawn is a generic cell's parts at the egg's size.

species.label: Syn3A
species.plain: A bacterium with a designed, minimised genome: 452 protein-coding genes kept from Mycoplasma mycoides, in a cell about 400 nm across with one membrane and no wall. It grows on its own in a rich medium, and its genome is smaller than that of any natural cell that does.

modelled.text: JCVI-syn3A is the project's minimal-cell track (decision D173, 14 November 2026), taken up from a note that proposes it as the first whole-cell validation organism for Cells: the decision adopted it as a track, run beside the current work. Nothing of it is in the engine yet: the project's record holds an evidence audit, capability probes of the engine as it stands, and a proposed first milestone, with no engine code written for it and nothing accepted. That milestone, on protein-free vesicles, tests membrane physics and not Syn3A.

proteins.membrane_from: the proteins that the species' own shelves place in or on the membrane

cap.membrane.note: Its one membrane holds the cell's ion and proton gradients. In the 2019 reconstruction of its metabolism the ATP synthase pushes protons out, against a passive leak of protons inwards; that is a model's reading, and no source read for this file measured the voltage of this strain.

cap.channels.why: No ion channel was found among its 455 proteins: none carries the signature of a channel family in Cells' catalogue, or of the bacterial channels for potassium, chloride, magnesium, water or membrane stretch, which the same search does find in other mollicutes. Its ions cross the membrane through transporters and pumps.

cap.pumps.note: Not the pumps of animal cells: it has no sodium-potassium pump. By its annotation, its ATP-driven ion movers are the ATP synthase, two P-type ATPases named as magnesium transporters, and a potassium uptake system.

cap.junctions.why: It lives as single cells and has no gap junctions: none of its proteins carries the signature of connexins or innexins.

cap.extracellular.note: Here it is the growth medium around the single cell, which the cell depends on. By the 2019 reconstruction of its metabolism it takes up glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and cholesterol from a rich medium.

cap.water.note: It has no cell wall: nothing but the membrane bounds its volume.

cap.calcium.why: It has no endoplasmic reticulum: it is a bacterium with a single membrane and no internal compartments, and none of its proteins carries the signature of the store's calcium pump or of its release channels.

cap.energy.note: Its ATP comes from fermenting sugar in the cytoplasm: in the 2019 reconstruction of its metabolism, central metabolism is the only source of ATP.

cap.mitochondria.why: It is a bacterium and has no mitochondria. Its ATP synthase sits in the cell membrane.

cap.circuits.note: At the chromosome, which lies in the cytoplasm: there is no nucleus. The 2019 paper notes how few regulatory proteins the minimised genome has left.

cap.grn.why: It forms no tissue, so there is nothing for gene networks to be coupled across. Gene expression within the one cell belongs with regulatory circuits.

cap.trafficking.why: It has no endoplasmic reticulum and no Golgi. By its annotation, new membrane proteins are put straight into the cell membrane by the Sec translocon and the YidC insertase.

cap.machines.note: About 500 ribosomes, with RNA polymerase, the ATP synthase and the protein translocon. None of its proteins carries the proteasome's signature; its annotation lists the proteases FtsH and Lon.

cap.secretion.note: By the 2019 reconstruction of its metabolism it releases the end products of sugar breakdown, lactate and acetate, into the medium and takes nutrients up. Signalling between its cells was not looked for.

cap.repair.note: The place would be its bare membrane. No source read for this file describes a membrane injury or its resealing in this organism.

cap.division.note: It grows and divides as a single cell. The division genes ftsZ and sepF are among 19 genes that were added to the smaller strain JCVI-syn3.0 to make it, which gave it back a regular shape; a review reports that seven of the 19 are needed together for normal division.

cap.replacement.why: It forms no tissue, so there is no neighbour for a new cell to replace.

cap.mechanics.why: It forms no sheet: its cells share no edges to pull on.

cap.sheet.why: It lives as single cells and forms no sheet of coupled cells.

species.label: M. pneumoniae
species.plain: A small bacterium of the human airways, among the smallest organisms that copy themselves: 688 proteins in the genome record frozen here, in a thin cell about 2 µm long with one membrane, no wall and an attachment organelle at one end.

levels.label: One cell
levels.note: Drawn as a rod 2 µm long and 0.2 µm across, the upper ends of the ranges given for the cell, with 300 ribosomes. The real cell is not a plain rod: it changes shape, and one end narrows into the attachment organelle, about 0.3 µm long, which this shape cannot show.

species.no_further_levels: A single-celled organism: each cell lives on its own, on the cells of its host, so it has no tissue, organ or body of its own.

facts.label: Shape and size
facts.value: a thin cell 1 to 2 µm long and 0.1 to 0.2 µm wide, of changeable shape, drawn out at one end into its attachment organelle; one paper gives its volume as 0.075 µm³

facts.label: Attachment organelle
facts.value: a membrane protrusion at one pole, 250 to 300 nm long, with an internal core; it carries the adhesins and leads the cell when it glides

facts.label: Envelope
facts.value: a cell membrane stiffened by sterols, and no cell wall; UniProt's curated entries of its proteins name one membrane, the cell membrane, and no outer one

facts.label: Inside
facts.value: a small prokaryote, among the smallest organisms that copy themselves: a bacterium, with no nucleus

facts.label: Chromosome
facts.value: one circle of 816,394 base pairs

facts.label: Genes
facts.value: 688 protein products in the genome record frozen here, the re-annotation of 2000; a review counts 687 genes, a re-annotation of 2015 has 694 reading frames, and UniProt has 686 entries

facts.label: Ribosome's size
facts.value: drawn as E. coli's ribosome, measured by the viewer from the coordinates of the Protein Data Bank's entry 7K00: as the ellipsoids of the same spread as their atoms, the large subunit 20.6 by 18 by 14.3 nm across and the small one 23.5 by 15.2 by 10 nm, their centres 10.4 nm apart, the whole 26.1 by 21.1 by 17.3 nm (its farthest atoms 26.8 by 24.3 by 20.6 nm). facts.label: Proteins
facts.value: about 120,000 protein molecules in a cell (120,700 on average over all samples), the sum over 528 kinds of protein measured by mass spectrometry, three quarters of all its kinds

facts.label: Doubling time
facts.value: about 8 hours in rich medium; 17.6 hours were measured in a serum-free medium

facts.label: Essential genes
facts.value: 342 of 694 genes essential, 93 needed for normal growth and 259 dispensable, by transposon mutagenesis

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: ATP from fermenting glucose, with lactate and acetate as end products; mycoplasmas lack the citric acid cycle

facts.label: Food
facts.value: glucose as its main fuel; it makes almost none of its own building blocks, no amino acids, vitamins or lipids among them, and takes them up

facts.label: Ion channels
facts.value: none found among its 688 proteins; one glycerol facilitator of the aquaporin family

facts.label: Division
facts.value: in two, by binary fission; the attachment organelle is duplicated first and takes part in the division

facts.label: Movement
facts.value: glides on surfaces, attachment organelle first, at up to 1 µm a second

facts.value: databases now list it as Mycoplasmoides pneumoniae; the papers cited call it Mycoplasma pneumoniae

cap.pumps.note: Not the pumps of animal cells: it has no sodium-potassium pump. By its annotation, its ATP-driven ion movers are the ATP synthase, one P-type ATPase whose ion is not known, and a potassium uptake system.

cap.junctions.why: It lives as single cells and has no gap junctions: none of its proteins carries the signature of connexins or innexins.

cap.extracellular.note: Here it is what surrounds the single cell: the surface of the airway cells it lives on, or a growth medium. The cell depends on it: it makes no amino acids, vitamins or lipids of its own and takes them up.

cap.water.note: It has no cell wall: nothing but the membrane bounds its volume. One of its proteins, GlpF, belongs to the family of water and glycerol channels.

cap.calcium.why: It has no endoplasmic reticulum: it is a bacterium with a single membrane and no internal compartments, and none of its proteins carries the signature of the store's calcium pump or of its release channels.

cap.energy.note: Its ATP comes from fermenting sugar in the cytoplasm, with lactate and acetate as end products; mycoplasmas lack the citric acid cycle.

cap.mitochondria.why: It is a bacterium and has no mitochondria. Its ATP synthase sits in the cell membrane.

cap.circuits.note: At the chromosome, which lies in the cytoplasm: there is no nucleus.

cap.trafficking.why: It has no endoplasmic reticulum and no Golgi. By its annotation, new membrane proteins are put straight into the cell membrane by the Sec translocon and the YidC insertase.

cap.machines.note: About 300 ribosomes, with RNA polymerase, the ATP synthase, the protein translocon and the machinery in its attachment organelle that lets it glide. None of its proteins carries the proteasome's signature; its annotation lists the proteases FtsH and Lon.

levels.label: One cell
levels.note: Drawn as a rod 2 µm long and 0.2 µm across, the upper ends of the ranges given for the cell, with 300 ribosomes. The real cell is not a plain rod: it changes shape, and one end narrows into the attachment organelle, about 0.3 µm long, which this shape cannot show.

ribosome.measured: The viewer's own measure from the entry's coordinates, by tools/measure_particle.py: each subunit as the ellipsoid of the same spread as its polymer atoms (model 1): along each of its own three axes a half-width of the square root of five times the atoms' variance; the farthest atoms beside it. The frame: origin at the centre of both subunits' atoms; y from the large subunit's centre to the small one's; x the whole particle's longest axis made square to y (the next one if the longest runs along y); z = x × y. The Protein Data Bank states no size.
ribosome.note: No entry of the Protein Data Bank for its own ribosome is named in the papers its file rests on: it is drawn at E. coli's measure.

cap.membrane.note: Its one membrane holds the cell's ion and proton gradients. In a model of its metabolism published in 2020 the ATP synthase runs in reverse and pumps protons out of the cell; that is the model's result, and no source read for this file measured the voltage.

cap.channels.why: No ion channel was found among its 688 proteins: none carries the signature of a channel family in Cells' catalogue, or of the bacterial channels for potassium, chloride, magnesium or membrane stretch, which the same search does find in other mollicutes. One protein, the glycerol facilitator GlpF, carries the signature of the family of water and glycerol channels; it is not an ion channel.

cap.pumps.note: Not the pumps of animal cells: it has no sodium-potassium pump. By its annotation, its ATP-driven ion movers are the ATP synthase, one P-type ATPase whose ion is not known, and a potassium uptake system.

cap.junctions.why: It lives as single cells and has no gap junctions: none of its proteins carries the signature of connexins or innexins.

cap.extracellular.note: Here it is what surrounds the single cell: the surface of the airway cells it lives on, or a growth medium. The cell depends on it: it makes no amino acids, vitamins or lipids of its own and takes them up.

cap.water.note: It has no cell wall: nothing but the membrane bounds its volume. One of its proteins, GlpF, belongs to the family of water and glycerol channels.

cap.calcium.why: It has no endoplasmic reticulum: it is a bacterium with a single membrane and no internal compartments, and none of its proteins carries the signature of the store's calcium pump or of its release channels.

cap.energy.note: Its ATP comes from fermenting sugar in the cytoplasm, with lactate and acetate as end products; mycoplasmas lack the citric acid cycle.

cap.mitochondria.why: It is a bacterium and has no mitochondria. Its ATP synthase sits in the cell membrane.

cap.circuits.note: At the chromosome, which lies in the cytoplasm: there is no nucleus.

cap.grn.why: It forms no tissue, so there is nothing for gene networks to be coupled across. Gene expression within the one cell belongs with regulatory circuits.

cap.trafficking.why: It has no endoplasmic reticulum and no Golgi. By its annotation, new membrane proteins are put straight into the cell membrane by the Sec translocon and the YidC insertase.

cap.machines.note: About 300 ribosomes, with RNA polymerase, the ATP synthase, the protein translocon and the machinery in its attachment organelle that lets it glide. None of its proteins carries the proteasome's signature; its annotation lists the proteases FtsH and Lon.

left_out.says: the barrel drawn for its molecular machines
left_out.reason: the picture drew it as a proteasome's core, which this cell does not have, and in a cell this small that barrel stood among the largest things drawn
left_out.why: On 17 November 2026 the user asked for the molecular machines' barrel to be left out of the bacteria's picture for now, as the map's protein assembly was left out of every species on 15 November; it read as an assembly of molecules, and stood among the largest things drawn. Its place and its note stay in this file: take the flag out and the barrel is drawn again.

cap.secretion.note: It releases lactate and acetate, the end products of its fermentation, and takes its nutrients up. Signalling between its own cells was not looked for.

cap.repair.note: The place would be its bare membrane. No source read for this file describes a membrane injury or its resealing in this organism.

cap.division.note: It divides in two as a single cell. Its attachment organelle is duplicated first and takes part in the division; the division gene ftsZ is in its genome.

cap.replacement.why: It forms no tissue, so there is no neighbour for a new cell to replace.

cap.mechanics.why: It forms no sheet: its cells share no edges to pull on. Its own movement, gliding on a surface, is not what this capability models.

cap.sheet.why: It lives as single cells and forms no sheet of coupled cells.

facts.label: Shape and size
facts.value: a thin cell 1 to 2 µm long and 0.1 to 0.2 µm wide, of changeable shape, drawn out at one end into its attachment organelle; one paper gives its volume as 0.075 µm³

facts.label: Attachment organelle
facts.value: a membrane protrusion at one pole, 250 to 300 nm long, with an internal core; it carries the adhesins and leads the cell when it glides

facts.label: Envelope
facts.value: a cell membrane stiffened by sterols, and no cell wall; UniProt's curated entries of its proteins name one membrane, the cell membrane, and no outer one

facts.label: Inside
facts.value: a small prokaryote, among the smallest organisms that copy themselves: a bacterium, with no nucleus

facts.label: Chromosome
facts.value: one circle of 816,394 base pairs

facts.label: Genes
facts.value: 688 protein products in the genome record frozen here, the re-annotation of 2000; a review counts 687 genes, a re-annotation of 2015 has 694 reading frames, and UniProt has 686 entries

facts.label: Ribosome's size
facts.value: drawn as E. coli's ribosome, measured by the viewer from the coordinates of the Protein Data Bank's entry 7K00: as the ellipsoids of the same spread as their atoms, the large subunit 20.6 by 18 by 14.3 nm across and the small one 23.5 by 15.2 by 10 nm, their centres 10.4 nm apart, the whole 26.1 by 21.1 by 17.3 nm (its farthest atoms 26.8 by 24.3 by 20.6 nm). The entry 5MDZ gives 25.6 by 21.2 by 18.5 nm, within 1.2 nm of it. No entry of the Protein Data Bank for its own ribosome is named in the papers its file rests on

facts.label: Ribosomes
facts.value: about 300 in a cell: the proteins of the ribosome were measured at a median of 300 copies in a cell, by mass spectrometry

facts.label: Proteins
facts.value: about 120,000 protein molecules in a cell (120,700 on average over all samples), the sum over 528 kinds of protein measured by mass spectrometry, three quarters of all its kinds

facts.label: Doubling time
facts.value: about 8 hours in rich medium; 17.6 hours were measured in a serum-free medium

facts.label: Essential genes
facts.value: 342 of 694 genes essential, 93 needed for normal growth and 259 dispensable, by transposon mutagenesis

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: ATP from fermenting glucose, with lactate and acetate as end products; mycoplasmas lack the citric acid cycle

facts.label: Food
facts.value: glucose as its main fuel; it makes almost none of its own building blocks, no amino acids, vitamins or lipids among them, and takes them up

facts.label: Ion channels
facts.value: none found among its 688 proteins; one glycerol facilitator of the aquaporin family

facts.label: Division
facts.value: in two, by binary fission; the attachment organelle is duplicated first and takes part in the division

facts.label: Movement
facts.value: glides on surfaces, attachment organelle first, at up to 1 µm a second

facts.label: Name
facts.value: databases now list it as Mycoplasmoides pneumoniae; the papers cited call it Mycoplasma pneumoniae

species.label: E. coli
species.plain: A rod-shaped bacterium of the animal gut: 4,403 proteins in UniProt's reference proteome of strain K-12, in a cell a few micrometres long with two membranes and a wall between them. It swims with flagella.

levels.label: One cell
levels.note: Drawn as a rod 2.5 µm long and 1 µm across: the picture's choice, within the ranges given for the cell. Its second membrane and its wall are drawn as clear shells around the cell membrane, and its 6,800 ribosomes are the low end of the range one paper gives. Its flagella and fimbriae are given as appendages, with the ranges their sources give; that the fimbriae stand all over the cell is the picture's choice, since no source read for this file says where they stand.

species.no_further_levels: A single-celled organism: each cell lives on its own, so there is no tissue, organ or body.

facts.label: Shape and size
facts.value: a straight rod; earlier work put its average length between 1.6 and 3.1 µm and its width at 0.7 to 1.1 µm, and one study measured 1.6 µm (cells at rest) to 3.9 µm (cells growing on a rich medium) in length and 1.26 µm in width

facts.label: Volume
facts.value: 1.5 to 4.4 femtolitres, by the conditions it grows in

facts.label: Envelope
facts.value: two membranes: the inner one separates the cytoplasm from the periplasm, the outer one the periplasm from the cell's surroundings; the cell wall lies between them

facts.label: Envelope's widths
facts.value: in frozen-hydrated sections of strain K-12, measured where the sections were least deformed, the inner membrane is 5.84 nm thick, the wall 6.35 nm and the outer membrane 6.87 nm; the space between the two membranes is 20.99 nm wide, and the wall lies 5.34 nm from the outer membrane, each the mean of eight measurements. Its authors give the periplasm's average compression in the sections as 32.47%. The paper does not say between which faces these widths run: taking them between the facing surfaces is this viewer's reading. Another paper measured 25.5 nm between the outer surface of the inner membrane and the inner surface of the outer membrane, at the middle of 31 whole cells of K-12, without osmoprotectants or fixation; the flagellar motor's close view takes a wider spacing from a third paper, of whole cells in hyperosmotic conditions, which its own file names

facts.label: Inside
facts.value: a bacterium, with no nucleus: its chromosome lies in a region of the cytoplasm that no membrane surrounds

facts.label: Chromosome
facts.value: one circle of 4,641,652 base pairs

facts.label: Proteins
facts.value: 4,403 in UniProt's reference proteome of strain K-12, every one with a reviewed entry

facts.label: Ribosome's size
facts.value: its ribosome, measured by the viewer from the coordinates of the Protein Data Bank's entry 7K00: as the ellipsoids of the same spread as their atoms, the large subunit 20.6 by 18 by 14.3 nm across and the small one 23.5 by 15.2 by 10 nm, their centres 10.4 nm apart, the whole 26.1 by 21.1 by 17.3 nm (its farthest atoms 26.8 by 24.3 by 20.6 nm). The entry 5MDZ gives 25.6 by 21.2 by 18.5 nm, within 1.2 nm of it

facts.label: Ribosomes
facts.value: between 6,800 and 72,000 in a cell, depending on its phase of growth, as one open paper sums up earlier estimates

facts.label: Movement
facts.value: swims with flagella that grow all over its surface, or does not move

facts.label: Flagella
facts.value: 1 to 5 on a cell in one study of single cells, and 3.4 on average by another paper; each a thread typically 5 to 10 µm long (7.5 µm by one measurement). Of the width the sources disagree: about 20 nm by one, 40 nm by another

facts.label: Where the flagella stand
facts.value: all over the cell body; the motor at the foot of each sits in the inner membrane, where its ring protein FliF and its stator proteins MotA and MotB are stated to be. 34 proteins are parts of the flagellum by the Gene Ontology terms UniProt gives them

facts.label: Type 1 fimbriae
facts.value: 200 to 500 on a cell by one paper's summary, each up to 1 µm long and about 7 to 10 nm wide, standing out from the outer membrane

facts.label: Chemotaxis
facts.value: 22 of its proteins carry UniProt's keyword for chemotaxis (aer, cheA, cheB, cheR, cheW, cheY, cheZ, dppA, fliG, fliJ, fliL, fliM, fliN, fliO, mglB, motA, motB, rbsB, tap, tar, trg and tsr), and 34 are parts of the flagellum by the Gene Ontology terms UniProt gives them

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: respiration and fermentation: it lives with or without oxygen

facts.label: Where it lives
facts.value: the lower gut of animals; it survives when released to the natural environment

facts.label: Ion channels
facts.value: none of the animal families listed in Cells' law inventory; 15 proteins of bacterial channel families (aqpZ, clcA, clcB, corA, glpF, kch, mscK, mscL, mscM, mscS, ybdG, ybiO, yfeO, ynaI and zntB)

facts.label: Signalling
facts.value: 64 proteins carry UniProt's keyword for two-component regulatory systems

facts.label: Strain
facts.value: K-12; the genome record is of its substrain MG1655, and UniProt's proteome is of the same genome assembly (GCA_000005845.2)

cap.grn.why: It forms no tissue, so there is nothing for gene networks to be coupled across. Gene expression within the one cell belongs with regulatory circuits.

cap.trafficking.why: It has no endoplasmic reticulum and no Golgi: no entry of its proteome states a place in either. By the names of their entries, its proteins cross or enter the inner membrane through the Sec and Tat translocases.

cap.machines.note: Its ribosomes, RNA polymerase, the ATP synthase, the protein translocases and the motor of its flagella. One of its proteins carries the signature of the proteasome's subunits: its entry names it "ATP-dependent protease subunit HslV".

Its place and its note stay in this file: take the flag out and the barrel is drawn again.

cap.secretion.note: Some of its proteins are stated to be secreted, and porins and transporters carry molecules across its two membranes. Signalling between its own cells was not looked for.

cap.repair.note: The place would be its envelope. No source read for this file describes an injury of it or its resealing in this organism.

cap.division.note: It divides as a single cell: its proteome names the cell division protein FtsZ.

cap.replacement.why: It forms no tissue, so there is no neighbour for a new cell to replace.

cap.mechanics.why: It forms no sheet: its cells share no edges to pull on. Its own movement, swimming with flagella, is not what this capability models.

cap.sheet.why: It lives as single cells and forms no sheet of coupled cells.

facts.label: Shape and size
facts.value: a straight rod; earlier work put its average length between 1.6 and 3.1 µm and its width at 0.7 to 1.1 µm, and one study measured 1.6 µm (cells at rest) to 3.9 µm (cells growing on a rich medium) in length and 1.26 µm in width

facts.label: Volume
facts.value: 1.5 to 4.4 femtolitres, by the conditions it grows in

facts.label: Envelope
facts.value: two membranes: the inner one separates the cytoplasm from the periplasm, the outer one the periplasm from the cell's surroundings; the cell wall lies between them

facts.label: Envelope's widths
facts.value: in frozen-hydrated sections of strain K-12, measured where the sections were least deformed, the inner membrane is 5.84 nm thick, the wall 6.35 nm and the outer membrane 6.87 nm; the space between the two membranes is 20.99 nm wide, and the wall lies 5.34 nm from the outer membrane, each the mean of eight measurements. Its authors give the periplasm's average compression in the sections as 32.47%. The paper does not say between which faces these widths run: taking them between the facing surfaces is this viewer's reading. Another paper measured 25.5 nm between the outer surface of the inner membrane and the inner surface of the outer membrane, at the middle of 31 whole cells of K-12, without osmoprotectants or fixation; the flagellar motor's close view takes a wider spacing from a third paper, of whole cells in hyperosmotic conditions, which its own file names

facts.label: Inside
facts.value: a bacterium, with no nucleus: its chromosome lies in a region of the cytoplasm that no membrane surrounds

facts.label: Chromosome
facts.value: one circle of 4,641,652 base pairs

facts.label: Proteins
facts.value: 4,403 in UniProt's reference proteome of strain K-12, every one with a reviewed entry

facts.label: Ribosome's size
facts.value: its ribosome, measured by the viewer from the coordinates of the Protein Data Bank's entry 7K00: as the ellipsoids of the same spread as their atoms, the large subunit 20.6 by 18 by 14.3 nm across and the small one 23.5 by 15.2 by 10 nm, their centres 10.4 nm apart, the whole 26.1 by 21.1 by 17.3 nm (its farthest atoms 26.8 by 24.3 by 20.6 nm). facts.label: Ribosomes
facts.value: between 6,800 and 72,000 in a cell, depending on its phase of growth, as one open paper sums up earlier estimates

facts.label: Movement

facts.label: Flagella

facts.label: Type 1 fimbriae

models.label: GARD assembly
models.plain: A model of how heredity could begin before genes: a small assembly of molecules of many types, in which the molecules inside speed the joining and leaving of others, so that a mix of types can grow, split in two and pass something of itself on. It is a model, not an organism: it has no cell, no shape, no place and no clock of real life. The preprint Plastic Heredity uses it.

notes.label: The law's two forms, in the engine's design (D192)
notes.text: As D192 records the checked finding: in a closed two-type world, the preprint's single-event kernel generically fails Kolmogorov's cycle criterion (a rank-one catalysis matrix is the exception); the original authors' kernel is not established either way; the preprint's vector-Poisson contracts were not tested; the preprint's driven runs are not affected; the pair-consistent form is exactly reversible. The engine builds both forms, and its first experiment measures the difference. The viewer shows the two side by side only for two runs of the engine of one world, and judges neither.

notes.label: Cells' own origin-of-life engine (D197)
notes.text: On 17 November 2026 the user decided that Cells builds its own first-principles engine, with GARD kept only for comparison (D197). GARD becomes one declared law set on general machinery: exact stochastic events, assemblies exchanging with a held phase, fission and lineage, a thermodynamic ledger and the run records. Cells' own engine takes its laws from physical chemistry: catalysis that is thermodynamically consistent, physical assemblies, and explicit sources of free energy. Its first choices were decided the same day (D199); nothing of it is built.

entities.label: Cell-owned compartments
entities.plain: A compartment that a cell owns, declared with its own identity and role: the first step toward closed compartments inside cells. Its first milestone landed on 15 November 2026 (feature request FR-1): the declaration alone, which leaves every existing run unchanged. Since the rework landed on 16 November 2026 it admits the kinds of piece the engine knows on a compartment's bounding membrane, under the implicit–explicit step only, and refuses any other kind. Since the evening of the same day it also admits FR-5's damage and pH condition, and a compartment whose admitted routes charge it can resume from its own checkpoint, in those worlds only (refusal 4 version 1.2, refusal 5 version 1.1). It records the first form of the compartment identity map, as information only. Its judged acceptances passed on 17 November 2026 in FR-4's and FR-5's protocols, 21 of 21 and 51 of 51 judged criteria, and on 18 November 2026 in FR-1's own, a closed compartment that exchanges species with its cell, 44 of 44, each against independent references written without the engine's code. Numerically qualified, on CPU only, within each scope line: for FR-4 and FR-5 the operator as built at 32a1d439, with refusal 4 version 1.2 and refusal 5 version 1.1; for FR-1 the neutral first version as built at 05a8d193, with the exchange, turnover and reactions operators, no ion route and a zero anchor on the compartment, under the implicit–explicit step (ARS) at 1 ms and RK4 at 0.1 ms. On 18 and 19 November 2026, after its judged runs, refusal 4 version 1.3 landed, which checks each move of a declared kind at the compartment's node against the step terms its law declares, and refusal 5 version 1.2, which admits a charge anchor where an admitted operator's routes charge the compartment, for FR-2; and membrane state now composes beside a compartment, but only together with FR-2's retrieval and recycling. Nothing was judged again, and the scope lines are unchanged.

entities.label: External modules
entities.plain: Packages maintained outside Cells could add laws and mechanisms that meet the same checks, accounting and execution contracts as the engine's own. Cells stays under the MIT licence, aiming at broad use (the user's direction, D180, 15 November 2026). Each part would be registered explicitly for one model build, then checked, assembled, compiled and run; registering a module that a model does not use changes nothing. The design note is still marked proposed. On 16 November 2026 the user, asking that others can easily add modules and laws by pull request, confirmed its five open decisions (D185). Contributed modules come first inside Cells, each in its own folder and namespace, under the MIT licence and with a named owner. A conformance kit shipped in Cells checks a module before its pull request; passing it means the kit's checks passed, not that the science is qualified. New physics still goes into the engine's source, as modules of its structure. The example module lives in this repository and is the template contributors copy. Development runs record an outside module's identity, and registered and judged runs also freeze its files. Two additions: the engine will write a declarations manifest, a list of every registered law, operator and kind with what it reads, writes and conserves, so that new modules appear in the documents and in this viewer's laws library without hand edits; and a contributor guide with a pull-request template. The four openings the design asked of the rework landed with it on 16 November 2026: kinds of piece are registered for one model build, exactly as an outside package would register them. Since 17 November 2026 laws and operators register the same way. Its first stage, one law from a separately installed package, is fifth in the plan's order after the landing, with the manifest and the guide. Since 17 November 2026 the import surface a module uses is on main, provisional, with no promise of stability until a first outside module arrives (D195), and the manifest is written (FR-12); since the evening of the same day the surface also exports the declaration types a family of its own needs: the law template, the family operator template and the record of a cited work; the kit, the example module and the guide come with the first stage. Still open: whether the project lists the modules that pass, and automatic checks on GitHub for outside pull requests. On 17 November 2026 the user set its first stage, with one installed external module and the question of a public stability promise, at low priority (D214); the plan keeps it in view as incomplete until its acceptance case passes. On 18 November 2026, with seam F's laws as modules, the surface became lazy: each name resolves on first use, so that a law's module can import it without importing the engine's internals, and a guard holds every module in the laws' folder to importing from Cells only the surface and other laws.

entities.label: Source layout by role
entities.plain: The user decided on 16 November 2026 (D188) that the engine's source takes the modular layout: each law a module of its own, grouped by mechanism (channels, junctions, pumps, routes, reactions, transport), and folders of their own for kinds, operators, models, numerics, execution, the registry, definitions and records. The older model families move into a folder of legacy code that nothing outside it imports. It is reached by two scripted moves, the older families first, each checked at every commit: the same collected tests, the compiled programs unchanged, all 113 saved worlds the same, and tiers 1 and 2 with no changed outcome. Its first step is done: a read-only tool lists the families from the import graph, and on 16 November 2026 the user settled the list (D189). Nine families stay active, among them four that registered protocols name, whose shared code moves into the modular core; 102 become legacy. Its design note, proposed, and the two scripts that plan, make and check the moves have been on main since 17 November 2026. The note's probe ran the whole cycle on a scratch copy of the tree, never merged: a family moved, a coupled kernel taken out and moved, and every check came out identical. Five refactors came first, on 17 November 2026: the legacy entry point (R1), computed module paths named in full (R2), the parts of seven older modules that active code reaches taken verbatim into the core's folder (R3), and two roots taken from the package instead of from a file's depth (R4, R5). The first move then landed on main the same day: the older families' 334 modules went into src/cells/legacy/ by its committed map, with no hand edits, keeping their sub-packages and their names, with no law, kind, operator or model identifier changed, and every gate held, a continuity resume across the move among them. Move 2, which puts the modular parts into the folders by role, came next, and no checkpoint crosses it (D195). First, as decided on 17 November 2026 (D198), the processes folder is dissolved as the first batch of removals: what an active entry point reaches moves, and the rest retires with its tests. The user decided the same day that the physical laws in it are first carried onto seam F's law template, even those not used yet, each with one reference check against saved outputs of the old code and a visible not-qualified status, after a table that sorts its 33 modules and at a lower priority than the gap-junction work; its numerical methods and geometry machinery wait for the engine's own geometry design, and the batch was held until the user accepted that split (D206). Later that evening the user decided that tested laws of the older code are ported to the active engine, the 54 law IDs behind 38 of the protein atlas's 48 units first, after a read-only inventory and one pilot family, below GARD and the gap-junction work in priority; this amends D196, and the retire batch's two laws join it. Mechanisms already owned are not ported as they stand: calcium handling folds into the cardiac laws, mitochondria into their own design, and the junction flux into FR-16. A law that becomes declared is not thereby qualified (D211). The user then set the chain (D213): the retire batch lands once its gate passes, then move 2, then the core-seams pass. The retire batch landed that evening: 33 source modules that no active entry point reached, 64 validation modules and 951 test IDs retired, and a tag holds every removed path. Its table sorted the 33 modules into 2 laws, 16 methods and 15 machinery modules. The two laws, the held charged-surface work law and conduction (J = σE) on the rectangular grid around cells, are to be rebuilt under D206 and D211, and their reference outputs are saved. Four input kernels that carry BETSE's conventions moved out of the engine, to the BETSE comparison tools. Move 2's prerequisites landed on 18 November 2026. A checkpoint written before a declared source move is refused by both loaders and by the continuity route, and the refusal names the tag where it restores; the made moves are declared in one module of the engine, which this part holds. The one-thread pin for linear algebra has one home, and the planner counts a family as active when the static model table has its row, so GARD's family stays active. For this the lead amended D195 the same day, and the user confirmed the amendment before move 2 landed: the layout a checkpoint was written in is read from its recorded source map, and GARD's frozen lineage reader refuses any changed source without naming the tag, which GARD's documentation names instead. Move 2 landed on 18 November 2026, after the origin-of-life engine's first laws (OL1): 117 modules moved by the committed map, with no hand edits in the move commit, into the laws' seven groups (channels, junctions, mechanics, pumps, reactions, routes and transport) and the folders for kinds, operators, definitions, execution, the registry and records; the processes and core folders dissolved, and no law, kind, operator or model identifier changed. The module above declares the move, with the tag of the tree before it. Its first gate failed, and the record says so: the move's rule for dotted names had rewritten five strings that are recorded data, not live references, and four files built moved paths from separate parts. Each was fixed in a commit of its own, and the landing gate held: tiers 1 and 2 with no changed outcome, all 113 saved worlds, crossrev's 9 of 9, every fingerprint of R1's 274 saved definitions, the pin in all 556 modules, the continuity acceptance test 13 of 13, and GARD's frozen first version and OL1's probes unchanged. No gate covers the BETSE evidence verifiers, the frozen release verifiers, the reports' closeouts or the geometry validation's source maps, and tier 3 is to be frozen again later. The moves are the first step of the order the user set (D194). Files are moved, not rewritten: putting each law's declaration, mathematics and citation in one module is a separate pass. Implemented and guarded: both moves are on main with their gates.

entities.label: GPU-native execution
entities.plain: What the rebuilt core already shows of the engine's GPU requirements. Since the rework landed on 16 November 2026, two hold, each shown by a test on main: a law that a world does not declare is absent from its compiled program, and a change of parameters alone reuses the compiled program and gives, bit for bit, what a fresh compile gives. Since the evening of the same day, a run of one world in windows can also check its saved rows on the device, on request: a second compiled program tests each window's rows, and any failure, or any account above half its bound, hands the window back to the usual checks on the host. This is opt-in and qualified on the CPU only. It is refused on a GPU until a GPU measurement exists, and for a world with an operator that retires cells, as division does, until a planted test exists. Every run made both ways gave the same results bit for bit, and no window was handed back. Against the host's checks on the same processors, the measured runs were 1.05 to 4.8 times as fast, and two long runs, whose host side is estimated, about 9 and 14 times. What is still to come on the GPU is a part of its own.

entities.label: Packed GPU execution
entities.plain: Many worlds of one structure packed into one batch on the GPU, to keep it busy. On the L4, one world of the 825-node tissue keeps about a quarter of the GPU's processors active; 128 worlds or more keep about 90% active. The same planner is meant to serve production ensembles. Its design was proposed on 15 November 2026, at the user's request, and a planner is built on a branch of its own. In a development run on the L4 on 16 November 2026, packed repeats were identical bit for bit, but packing alone moved some small flux and ledger values by up to 1.6e-8 relative, more than the criterion set for it. The same day this was traced to rounding amplified by the conditioning of the field solve: the moved values are small differences of potentials. The direction ruled judges each field at 1e-12 of the scale it is computed from, with an empirical cap for the outside network's ledgers and an exact check of what the host computes from the state; it is not frozen until a held-out pass on the merged code. The four seams it asked of the core landed with the windows lane on the evening of 16 November 2026: arguments built for each window, a world named on every refusal, a typed refusal for memory, and an opt-in mode that sets a refused world aside and carries on with the others. The planner merges after its own gate, and its one-time GPU qualification runs on the merged code. Not on main.

entities.label: One thread for linear algebra
entities.plain: So that a run on ordinary processors gives the same bits however many processors it is given. The core found on 16 November 2026 that a run's bits followed the number of threads its linear-algebra libraries use, which follows the processors a run is given, and the user decided the same evening (D190) to run them on one thread. It merged into main just after midnight on 17 November 2026: every such library runs on one thread from the first import of the engine, and again at each of the eight places a run starts; the counts are read back, and a run is refused if any is not at one. Run manifests record each library's version, kernel and thread count, and checkpoints written before the pin still restore. With it, the 825-node world gives the same bits on 1, 2 and 4 processors. Runs of large worlds on several processors give up the threaded part of the step's factorization, 21 ms of the 825-node world's 91 ms step on one processor; one-processor and GPU runs are unchanged. Since move 2's prerequisites landed on 18 November 2026 the pin at import has one home, the engine package's first module, as D190 first said: all 530 modules measured are pinned, and a planted control unpins all 47 sampled. At move 2's landing gate the same day the pin held in every module, 556 of 556, and the pin's own module moved with the execution modules. Implemented and guarded.

entities.label: Human cardiac laws
entities.plain: The laws of a human heart muscle cell from the ventricle, so that the engine can run a paced human cell. The user brought them forward on 16 November 2026 (D183), as a lane of their own on the rebuilt tissue model. Their design note, on main since the same day and still proposed, sets out eight new channel laws, two new transporter cycles (the sodium–calcium exchanger and the sodium–potassium pump), a calcium release law, a rapid calcium buffer and a calcium-dependent enzyme, CaMKII, with calcium handling moved into the tissue model in pools that share the cell's potential. Each law is named by its mechanism, not by a protein. The choices were made the same day (D184): the equations and parameters of O'Hara and Rudy's 2011 model of the endocardial cell; that cell type first, and others later as sets of parameters; Hodgkin–Huxley gates for the sodium current; and 310 K. Each law would be checked under voltage clamp against an independent reference. The user approved a whole-cell comparison over one beat for that model only: against an independent reference written from the paper, judged, and against the published model, run unmodified and outside the engine, keeping only its saved outputs, reported and not judged. No engine code is written yet. They are built in step 3 of the order the user set on 16 November 2026 (D194), after D188's moves and one pass over the core's shared seams, in parallel with operator composition and finite fuel. The human living-cell loop waits for these laws.

entities.label: Laws as declared pieces
entities.plain: Before the rework, the tissue model's channel laws were a closed table: every law was computed for every channel population and the right one selected afterwards, even in a world with no channels. Since the rework landed on 16 November 2026, each of its five channel laws, its junction law and its two pump laws is declared once, under a fixed code, and a world's program is built from the laws that world declares: a law that is not declared is absent from the program. A probe had found that separating the laws moves no result: in seven worlds every value at every step stayed the same bit for bit, with smaller programs. Since 17 November 2026 each is declared on the law template, and since 18 November 2026 each stands in a module of its own, with its kernels: the core pass's seam F, laws as modules. Such a module registers nothing itself; the law registry's loader registers its law and records the module, and the older families' modules re-import the moved names, so that they run the one copy. Five more modules hold the laws of the Kv1 port pilot (D211). Since 19 November 2026 the tissue model's parser reads its channel table from the law registry, so all five are registered as its channel laws, codes 5 to 9, and the older Kv1 catalogue builds its tables from their numbers. The same day an always-open chloride leak joined them as code 10, one of the general features that real use cases found missing (D228, item 3): the tissue model's table of valences admits chloride at −1, and a chloride conductance sits on a patch beside its others, switched by the population's availability. The tissue model's own module keeps the tables its readers use, read from the registry, and seam D's switch: for each of the tissue model's classes of mover, channels, junctions, membranes, pumps and calcium pumps, a world may pick the trapezoid booking of heat beside the default, and a world that picks none keeps its programs. New kinds of piece join through the kind interface, and the operators declare what they read, change and book through the operator contract. Implemented and guarded: tests on main hold each law to its module and to the registry, and each of the five Kv1 laws to two references and to the older catalogue's numbers, and the landing's gates held, with no changed outcome in tiers 1 and 2, all 113 saved worlds and crossrev's ten sets. A test holds that a chloride population moves what a chloride patch does, and at the chloride leak's landing tiers 1 and 2 showed no changed outcome and crossrev's eleven sets were identical.

entities.label: Kind interface
entities.plain: How a new kind of piece joins the tissue model. A kind is one module's contribution: its own fields, and hooks that the tissue model calls at fixed points of its step. Each kind registers itself on a registry that belongs to one model build, exactly as a package from outside Cells would, and a kind that a world does not declare changes nothing. Its name carries a namespace, so an outside kind cannot collide with a built-in one, and the order in which kinds add their fields is fixed by their sorted names. On main since the rework landed on 16 November 2026, with three built-in kinds: passive routes, a rapid proton buffer and transporters. Since the evening of the same day there are two more, for feature request FR-5: the damage of a membrane patch and a pH condition, which act on routes only through the routing door. A test on main registers a planted kind from outside the engine's source and runs it through every seam, and two kinds whose reads of one row could disagree are refused when a world is built. On the evening of 16 November 2026, with the core's next lane, it gained controls that change on a schedule, a routing door through which one kind's factors scale another's routes, and the terms finite fuel needs in the energy accounts. Since 18 November 2026 a kind writes only its own resolved, declared fields, its initial values, derivatives and control outputs, and a planted write to another's field is refused where the model is built and where it is traced: one of two boundary fixes that an external adviser's architecture review asked for, landed before move 2 as an exception to D195's order (D214). With the core pass's first landings on 18 November 2026, the kind contract gained the declarations its seams need, each checked at registration: a field's energy role, the heat bookings a kind admits, its partition roles and its ledgers, and the class of a kind's rates, which the tissue model now imports from it; and the core fixes, carried across the second source move, added a kind's material slope to the step's rule: an explicit stage is refused where the step times the largest slope at a node exceeds the explicit step's bound (D4). On 19 November 2026 it gained presence fields, which let a kind stand beside a closer, gated by its host's activity, with the built-in transporter declaring its own so that no kind code changed; the kinds' own ledgers, read into the inner model's checks; and one lifecycle for kinds' state at division and retirement, driven by each field's role. On 19 November 2026 the check that each kind field's array matches its declared axes where the tissue model binds it landed (D228, item 6), and the presence gate came to host channel and face slots, so that a kind with presence on channel populations or faces is admitted beside a closer. Implemented and guarded.

entities.label: Law template and registry
entities.plain: How a law is declared and found. Since 17 November 2026 every law declares one record of its interface's type, a channel, membrane cycle, passive route, binding or junction law, with what runs it, where it comes from, a citation where one is cited, and the units and signs of its fields. Laws register on a registry that belongs to one model build, and a kind finds its laws by interface and host; a law that no definition declares changes nothing. The tissue model's laws use it, sixteen of them rows of its own since 19 November 2026. The template stays provisional until a first outside module arrives (D195). Since the core pass's landings of 18 and 19 November 2026 a cycle law may carry its general form, and a binding law the general closure's kernels, its free energy among them (seams A and C). Since the evening of 17 November 2026 the set of law interfaces is open to the engine's own families: a family declares its own in the static model table, each a type built on the template that checks its own fields. Since 18 November 2026 a law declared in a module of its own is listed as a law home in the model table, and the loader that registers it records its module; the cycle and route law types carry the step terms that the operators' admission reads, each the name of a kernel or none: a charge slope and a material slope for the step's rule, and bounds at definition for a charged and a neutral row. Declared extension, a law, operator or model that the engine records and checks as an extension of another, is on the backlog, requested and not scoped (FR-14, D205): today a subclass registers under an ID of its own, and nothing records or checks it as an extension. Implemented and guarded.

entities.label: Origin-of-life laws (OL1)
entities.plain: Landed for development, not judged (18 November 2026). The four laws of the origin-of-life engine's first milestone (OL1), physical chemistry in an assembly: mass action for a step's encounter, in exact molecule counts (cells.stochastic_mass_action@1); catalysis as a factor on the state a step and its reverse share, so that a catalyst speeds or slows both alike and never moves an equilibrium (cells.transition_state_factor@1); and two terms of one free energy of the counts, ideal mixing, exact in the counts, and the membrane's regular mixing (cells.ideal_mixing@1, cells.regular_mixing@1). Each step comes as a forward and reverse pair, the reverse rate from the exact change of that free energy, so every pair keeps local detailed balance. Each law is declared on the family's own interfaces of seam F's template, with the works it cites, and the engine's declarations list all four. They follow the lead's rulings written into the design note. Against OL5's references, registered before any engine output, they passed 6 of 6 rows on 18 November 2026. Nothing is judged under a registered protocol, and nothing is compared with experiment. Implemented and guarded: on main with their tests, among them the laws' registration and the kernel's detailed balance, in tiers 1 and 2 of the engine's test tiers.

entities.label: Transporters and proton buffer
entities.plain: Two kinds of piece of the tissue model, on main since the rework landed on 16 November 2026. A transporter is a population on a membrane patch that spends one ATP per cycle to move a species from one side to the other: an uncharged one, or protons, as the pump that acidifies a compartment does (feature request FR-4). In this round its fuel is held constant, as rows of the shared inventory that are read and never used up; finite fuel is refused until a later step. The rapid proton buffer sets, at every stage of a step, how many of a node's protons are free and how many are bound to the buffers declared there, so that laws can read the pH while the node's charge stays as stored. Implemented and guarded. Both ran in FR-4's judged acceptance on 17 November 2026, which passed all 21 judged criteria; its scope line names the compartment operator as built at 32a1d439. On 19 November 2026 the core pass gave both a general form, for development, not judged. The transporter became seam A's general cycle kind, which runs any declared cycle law, each law's modes and kinetics given as data by a cycle form, in a module of forms that binds no law of its own; it landed with its comparison against the code-blind references for seam A. The buffer's closure became rapid_binding@1, seam C's rapid-equilibrium binding of several ligands on binders of several forms, run in whole worlds and with its free energy booked. Neither general form ran in a judged acceptance. Tests on main hold the cycle forms, the cycle kind against seam A's references, and the binding closure against seam C's references at every registered state. On 19 and 20 November 2026 the cycle kind gained two cycle laws, an electrogenic sodium-coupled anion symporter in two forms, a general feature a real use case found missing (D228, item 1), cited, and neither judged: a factored form with no fuel, its sodium count a declared parameter from 1 to 4, refused at a compartment's node; and its version 2, a kinetic diagram of eight states with two sodium ions per cycle, its rate constants a definition's values. The kind also gained schedules of a population's availability (D228, item 5) with its population bound in log space, a trapezoid booking of its heat, readouts of the proton-motive force, moved fuel at a binding closure's nodes, and its standard free energies declared as entries the species registry checks; and on 20 November 2026 a fourth kinetic form, monomial, landed as groundwork for the mitochondria work, with no law of that form yet. The general binding closure's booked energy term is now formed from increments through the closure's dual, which removed a rounding floor that had failed the step-doubled energy check's order condition in buffered worlds. Tests on main hold both symporter laws.
